author: Reel Ken
title: I recently wrote an article on Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) that wa
text:
I recently wrote an article on Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) that wasn't the everyday typical article. It was designed to discuss the idiosyncratic nature of high-beta stocks and help investors avoid some very common mistakes. Several readers commented that they sell naked puts and wondered why that wasn't covered. I pointed out that selling puts on high-beta stocks like AAPL was not as simple as investors realize, and it necessitates another article to explore it properly.
First, we must start with the most basic definition of a high beta stock. Simply stated, it is a stock that is more volatile than the overall market. The overall market has a beta of 1.00, and a stock with a beta of 1.20 is considered 20% more volatile. There is no really fixed threshold that defines how high the beta of a stock must be before it should be classified "high beta". Is it 1.10? 1.20?
AAPL's beta, as determined by Reuters and Yahoo Finance is 1.31, and that certainly qualifies, in my mind, as high beta. So, I choose to use AAPL as a surrogate for high beta stocks.
Volatility can be challenging to even the most seasoned investor. In exchange for tolerating AAPL's volatility, investors are offered the potential for outsized gains.
This is dramatically illustrated by a simple chart comparing AAPL to the S&P 500 over the last 12 months.

As can be seen, AAPL exhibited three drops of nearly 9% each time, and each of those drops took place over just a matter of weeks. The rises, though substantial, took a little longer to materialize. But even after the most recent drop, AAPL handily outperformed the S&P 500.
